title: What I've been working on, and what I learned
byline: Ray's update, with the numbers behind it
why: I want Kong Royale to run smoothly for everyone, on any laptop and in any browser, Safari too, without crashing mid-match. So every change has to be proven on real machines before it ships, and every number on this page says where it came from.

kinds.model: from a network model, not a real network yet

wins.head: Safari finishes a whole match on a 16 GB Mac
wins.beforeText: Reached Safari's limit 82 s after landing, at 8.5 GB
wins.afterText: Reaches the results screen, peaking at 6.9 to 7.3 GB
wins.plain: Safari gives one tab about 8.5 GB on a 16 GB Mac, and I set out to fit inside that. The game now keeps at most 4 far-away locations loaded instead of 10, and a full match ends on the results screen.
wins.source: Mac mini M4 16 GB, Safari, main 3248912 (2 runs) against main 1ee1f52 (1 run); tools/dashboard/story.json, project drive handoffs/safari-growth/pr160/README.md
wins.changeText: from reaching the limit to finishing the match

wins.head: Tuk-tuks draw in fewer pieces
wins.plain: Tuk-tuks were the biggest source of draw calls on my test route. Each part was split into pieces for no visual reason, so I merged each part into one mesh per material.
wins.source: Mesh count in client/src/actors/tuktuk.ts, with same-camera stills (2 of 3 views identical, 1 pixel differs in the third); Captain drive reports/KONG-68.md

wins.head: The Murk's tree crowns draw in one go
wins.beforeText: About 170 draws a frame for the crowns
wins.plain: Each 36 m cell of crowns was three meshes. I batched the cells, so the whole canopy is one draw per pass.
wins.source: Draw counts from Mango Market; on an RTX laptop walk-town draws went 655 to 513 (p50) with frame times inside the run-to-run spread; Captain drive handoffs/upstream/batch14/murk/bodies/murk-crown-batch.md

wins.head: Safari at High is smoother
wins.plain: At High on a Retina screen, Safari's frame lands just past 16.7 ms and snaps to 30 fps. The fix lowers only the 3D resolution while the game misses the refresh, then raises it again.
wins.source: Safari 27.0.1 on a Mac, High, DPR 2, main 9cc83fa (n=4) against the PR (n=5); Captain drive reports/KONG-82.md

wins.head: Inputs keep flowing on a lossy connection
wins.unit: ms of input delay beyond ping, slowest 1%
wins.beforeText: 214 ms on WebSockets at 250 ms ping and 1% loss (108 ms at 150 ms ping)
wins.afterText: 48.2 ms on WebTransport (48.8 ms at 150 ms ping)
wins.plain: On WebSockets one lost packet holds up every input behind it. The new optional WebTransport path sends every unacknowledged input in each packet, so the next packet repairs a lost one. These runs used real network stacks over an emulated path; next is the real-player A/B.
wins.source: Netpath matrix: real kernel TCP and QUIC over an emulated path, n=10 per arm (9 or 10 completed), main d83729f, ack minus RTT p99; project drive handoffs/KONG-wt/netpath/2026-11-06-d83729f/netpath-matrix.md

wins.head: Low-memory mode uses 40% less graphics memory
wins.unit: MB of graphics memory at the title
wins.beforeText: 3,141 MB by default (4,206 MB in the plane)
wins.afterText: 1,894 MB in low-memory mode (2,226 MB in the plane)
wins.plain: Low-memory mode at first only waited to load far-away areas. It now frees them and draws a cheap stand-in, so Safari keeps at most 4 far-away locations loaded instead of 10.
wins.source: Mac mini M4, Metal, WebGL MB, farimp re-gate 2 (KONG-54), main fbe5559; project drive handoffs/farimp-regate2-metal/

wins.head: Less memory held twice
wins.unit: MB of shape copies in a match
wins.beforeText: 219 MB kept in main memory after upload
wins.plain: Meshes kept a copy of their shape in main memory after the graphics card had it. They now drop it and rebuild it only if the browser resets the graphics. It is behind a flag today; turning it on for everyone waits on a real-GPU check.
wins.source: SwiftShader on a cloud machine, tools/performance/memory.mts; project drive handoffs/geofree-default/README.md (PR #268, open)

lessons.head: One thread isn't really the wall
lessons.plain: Every WebGL engine sends its draw calls from one JavaScript thread, three.js included. But the browser already does the heavy driver work in its own GPU process, and the WebGL calls are only about 10% of my main thread. What fills it is my own code around each draw: about 16 µs a draw on my RTX laptop and 12 µs on the Mac mini, against about 1.5 µs for plain three.js in a benchmark. That gap is mine to fix.
lessons.source: RTX laptop, Chrome D3D11, 1080p High, walk-town tour medians (765 draws) and 4 CPU profiles; Mac mini M4 Chrome tour (755 draws); three.js floor from a 1,500-mesh microbenchmark on a cloud machine; Captain drive reports/KONG-89.md

lessons.head: Where my main thread goes
lessons.plain: Share of main-thread busy time on the RTX laptop walking through town. three.js drawing is the biggest piece; my game's own update is next.
lessons.source: 4 Chrome CPU profiles, RTX laptop, walk-town, bucketed by call tree; Captain drive reports/KONG-89.md

lessons.head: Small wins hide in the noise
lessons.plain: A 5-run frame-time test can't see a change smaller than about 5%. So I price each idea with a profile and object counts before I spend GPU time on it, and a PR can say "no clear change" and still be a real saving.
lessons.source: Noise band of 5-run A/Bs from reports/KONG-68.md and KONG-89.md; the #265 result from reports/KONG-82.md; freezing static nodes is an estimate (0.15 to 0.3 ms of 18.9 ms) from reports/KONG-89.md

lessons.head: The same effect costs different amounts on different machines
lessons.plain: The light rays are nearly free on my RTX laptop but likely cost a few ms on a Mac at Retina resolution. In Safari that can be the difference between 60 and 30 fps, because frames snap to the screen's refresh. These are estimates: there is no per-pass GPU timer yet, and adding one is on my list.
lessons.source: Fetch counts for the quarter-resolution light-ray pass in client/src/world/atmos/post.ts; Captain drive reports/KONG-89.md

lessons.head: Safari plays by its own rules
lessons.plain: Safari caps how much memory one tab can use: around 8.5 GB on a 16 GB Mac, where I saw tabs reach the limit at 8.4 to 8.8 GB. Its frame timing even fooled my refresh-rate detection, so I fixed that too.
lessons.source: Safari page memory on a Mac mini M4 16 GB; tools/dashboard/story.json; the limit range from Captain drive reports/KONG-62.md

lessons.head: Freeing memory takes ownership
lessons.plain: Low-memory mode at first only waited to load far-away areas, so after a few km you were back to full memory. It now frees far areas and draws a cheap stand-in in their place.
lessons.source: Locations held at once in a Safari match on a Mac mini M4 16 GB, before and after eviction; tools/dashboard/story.json; Chrome D3D11 growth trace in project drive handoffs/lowmem-growth-d3d11/README.md
